question: Where does the hybrid night frame spend its time, and what would a cheaper material buy?
instrument: Vsync disabled (--disable-gpu-vsync --disable-frame-rate-limit), so a frame time is continuous instead of quantised to multiples of 16.7 ms; both worlds measured in one browser session so the machine state is shared; the product pixel ratio 1.15 (canvas 1655x1035) unchanged, light and geometry unchanged. Frame budget for 60 Hz is 16.7 ms.

nightFrameMs.note: "fragment hidden" is lower than the voxel product because the hybrid world excludes the five blocks the fragment replaces: hiding it leaves a hole. The fragment's own cost is therefore hybrid minus voxel, 2.85 ms, not hybrid minus hidden.

localLights.note: the dominant term, and the product pays it too (11.9 of its 12.0 ms night frame)

fragmentWithLights.note: hybrid 14.8 minus voxel 12.0 at the same resolution

fragmentWithoutLights.note: hybrid 3.59 minus voxel 3.34: the fragment costs almost nothing on its own

glassLayers.note: hiding every transparent mesh of the fragment

attribution.conclusion: The fragment's night cost is its pixels being shaded by sixteen point lights in a forward renderer, not the material's texture detail. Intensity is not a lever: three.js compiles the light count into the shader, so zeroing eight lights changed nothing (14.82 vs 14.97 ms). Only the light budget or the pixel count moves this number.

resolutionScaling.note: the frame scales with pixel count (ratio 1.35 measured against 1.32 of pixels), which is what a fill-bound frame does

levers.costs: every surface in the fragment flattens
a dimmer street, city-wide, at High
